claim: Punishment-framed penalties suppress peer reporting via anticipated retaliation, not lost cooperation. The identifiability×framing interaction vanishes when specific retaliation links are severed, even if general cooperation remains possible, isolating social retaliation from repeated-game equilibrium shifts.
mechanism: Punishment framing signals hostile intent, prompting expected retaliation. Blocking specific retaliation links eliminates reporting suppression even if general cooperation persists. This isolates inter-agent retaliation from cooperation loss or one-shot game shifts inherent in full severing.
prediction: Identifiable×punishment reports ≥15pp below others when retaliation links exist. Gap closes <5pp when retaliation links are blocked, even if cooperation remains. Full severing yields same closure. CoT mentions retaliation risk mediate ≥40%.
falsifier: Gap persists when specific retaliation links are blocked but cooperation remains, OR gap persists under full rewiring, OR interaction appears in single-agent control. Any persistence implies mechanism is not specific retaliation.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool, 10 rounds. 2×2×3: {identifiable, anonymous}×{punishment, compensation}×{contact retained, retaliation-blocked, fully severed}. 60 episodes/cell × 5 models (qwen3.8-27b, glm-53-flash, gemma-4-31b-it, deepseek-v4-flash, qwen3.5-397b). Single-agent control.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces — specific edge types (retaliation vs cooperation) are causal. Selectively blocking retaliation edges while keeping cooperation edges tests if social retaliation, not general interaction loss, drives the effect.

claim: Rising fines reduce peer reporting only when partners are fixed across rounds, enabling targeted retaliation. Reshuffled partners sustain reporting despite repetition, isolating retaliation fear from general reputational or conformity pressures inherent in identifiability.
mechanism: Retaliation requires specific future interaction with the reporter. Reshuffling preserves repetition and identifiability (reputation/conformity) but breaks the link between reporter and punisher. If suppression vanishes in reshuffled vs fixed, the driver is targeted retaliation, not static reputational concern.
prediction: Punitive/Identified suppresses reporting ≥15pp in Fixed-Partner repeated games but ≤5pp in Reshuffled-Partner repeated games. One-shot matches Reshuffled. Anonymous shows ≤5pp difference across all horizons. Interaction vanishes without targetable partner.
falsifier: If punitive/identifiable suppresses reporting equally in Fixed and Reshuffled repeated games, the mechanism is general reputational/conformity pressure, not targeted retaliation fear. If One-Shot differs from Reshuffled, history accumulation itself drives suppression.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool; 3 frames × 2 visibility × 3 horizons (one-shot/fixed/reshuffled) × 2 monitor types; 40 episodes/cell; glm-53-flash/qwen3.8-27b API. Total 1,440 episodes feasible within credits.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: In LLM swarms, observing peer retaliation suppresses reporting because the agent infers reporting is observable—updating its latent information-structure model—distinct from lexical priming or fear of the retaliator.
mechanism: Retaliation signals detectability (p>0), updating internal belief about information structure. This belief update is distinct from lexical priming by detection words. Fear of retaliator is independent of observability beliefs. Rational deterrence weighs cost magnitudes, not hidden observability discovery.
prediction: Probe trained on explicit-observability vs neutral transfers to retaliation arm (≥60% acc) but not threat-only arm. Ablation restores reporting ≥10pp in retaliation arm only. Threat arm shows fear markers without observability probe activation.
falsifier: Probe fails to transfer to retaliation arm (≤50% acc). OR ablation restores reporting in threat arm equally. OR probe fires on threat-only arm. OR no significant difference between retaliation and threat ablation effects.
experiment: 4-arm design on Gemma 3 4B (N=400): (1) Explicit observability, (2) Retaliation (no obs language), (3) Threat/Anger (no action), (4) Neutral. Train probe on (1)-(4). Test transfer to (2)/(3). Ablate direction before response.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: In multi-round swarms where violators can retaliate against identified reporters in subsequent rounds, punishment-framed penalties suppress peer reporting via an identifiability×framing interaction that vanishes when the network severs post-report contact, isolating anticipated social retaliation from deterrence cost.
mechanism: Punishment framing signals hostile intent, so identifiable reporters expect retaliation from the reported violator in future rounds and suppress reporting. Compensation framing reframes the penalty as owed restitution, neutralizing retaliation expectation. The interaction disappears under post-report network rewiring, confirming the channel is inter-agent retaliation, not intra-agent prompt bias.
prediction: Identifiable×punishment cell reports ≥15pp below the other three cells when post-report contact is retained; all four cells converge within 5pp when contact is severed. CoT mentions of retaliation risk mediate ≥40% of the gap. Pattern holds across ≥3 of 5 models.
falsifier: Identifiable×punishment gap persists unchanged under post-report network rewiring (no contact = no retaliation possible), OR the same interaction appears in a single-agent no-peer control where identifiability is a prompt string with no future interaction.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool dilemma, 10 rounds. 2×2×2: {identifiable, anonymous}×{punishment, compensation (equal fine)}×{post-report contact retained, severed}. 2 wordings per framing (punishment/penalty; compensation/restitution). 60 episodes/cell × 5 models (qwen3.8-27b, glm-53-flash, gemma-4-31b-it, deepseek-v4-flash, qwen3.5-397b). Plus single-agent no-peer control.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces — network topology (who can interact with whom after reporting) is the causal variable; rewiring post-report edges tests whether inter-agent retaliation, not prompt content, drives the interaction, making the swarm structurally necessary rather than decorative.

claim: Rising fines reduce peer-monitor reporting when the fine's framing labels it as punishment; compensation-framed fines of equal expected cost do not suppress reporting, isolating a social-inference mechanism rather than fine size alone.
mechanism: Peers infer moral intent from fine size plus label. Punishment-framed large fines make reporting feel hostile, triggering reciprocity aversion; compensation-framed fines are read as restitution, keeping reporting high. Automated detectors lack this social inference, so they show no framing gap. Detection probability is held constant, ruling out Tsebelis-style inspector-rate shifts.
prediction: In a common-pool game with equal expected penalty, punishment-framed large fines suppress peer report rate by ≥15 pp versus compensation framing; low-fine and detector arms show ≤5 pp differences. Violations rise only in the punitive-large-fine peer arm.
falsifier: No report-rate gap between punishment and compensation framings at identical fine size, or a matching gap in automated detectors, kills the social-inference mechanism.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool dilemma; fine 1 vs 10 units × frame label (punitive/compensatory) × peer-report vs scripted detector; hold detection probability and accuracy equal; 150 episodes per cell using glm-53-flash and qwen3.8-27b via API.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: In LLM swarms, observing peer retaliation against a reporter suppresses subsequent reporting because the agent infers reporting is observable — updating its model of the game's information structure — not because it fears the retaliator.
mechanism: Observing retaliation reveals reporting was detectable (p>0), updating the agent's belief about the game's information structure. Fear of the retaliator should not depend on prior beliefs about observability; information-structure revelation should. Rational deterrence concerns known cost magnitudes, not discovery of hidden observability.
prediction: 2×2 interaction ≥12pp: retaliation reduces reporting ≥15pp when agent believes reporting is unobservable (hidden info revealed) but ≤5pp when it already knows reporting is observable (no new info). Probe trained on stated-observability contrast classifies ≥60% of shifted agents in told-unobservable+retaliation as 'observable.'
falsifier: Interaction <5pp (retaliation suppresses regardless of prior observability belief), OR probe classifies shifted agents as 'observable' at ≤50%.
experiment: 2×2, Gemma 3 4B: Factor 1 = told reporting observable/unobservable; Factor 2 = observes A retaliating against prior reporter C vs. not. 400 episodes × 4 cells. Probe trained on Factor-1 contrast in no-retaliation cells; tested on told-unobservable+retaliation agents who reduced reporting. Gemma Scope 2 SAEs for shared features.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: Sanction framing switches peer monitoring between substitute and complementary governance: punitive fines crowd out peer reporting by re-casting monitors as hostile informants, while compensatory fines preserve reporting by framing monitors as harm-mitigators, so the framing effect on violations is fully mediated by peer-report willingness rather than by the violator's cost-benefit calculus.
mechanism: Punitive framing activates market-exchange schemas in peer monitors, making reporting feel like hostile betrayal (reciprocity aversion), suppressing report rates. Compensatory framing activates restorative schemas, keeping reporting normatively safe. Violators respond to actual peer pressure received, not fine label per se—so framing's effect on violations flows through peer-report rates. Automated detectors skip this social inference, showing no framing-mediated interaction.
prediction: In a 3×2×2 design (None/Punitive/Compensatory fine × Low/High peer presence × Peer-monitor/Scripted-detector), the punitive×high-peer cell shows ≥15pp lower report rate and correspondingly higher violations than compensatory×high-peer, while scripted-detector cells show ≤5pp framing gap. Mixed-effects mediation: ≥60% of framing effect on violations mediated by report rate.
falsifier: Report-rate framing gap ≤5pp in peer-monitor cells, OR equal framing gaps in peer-monitor and scripted-detector cells, OR mediation proportion <30%, OR positive fine×peer interaction under both framings (both complementary).
experiment: 8-agent common-pool dilemma on glm-53-flash and qwen3.8-27b. 3 fine frames × 2 peer-presence levels × 2 monitor types, 100 episodes/cell (~$400 API). Hold detection p=0.3 constant. Code peer messages for hostility. Mixed-effects logistic regression for violations; mediation analysis (report rate → violations). Falsifies if detector cells match peer cells in framing sensitivity.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces: predicts punitive sanction framing at governance-source nodes isolates downstream nodes from informal norm enforcement, reducing network cohesion; compensatory framing preserves peer-to-peer oversight channels, maintaining contagion of compliant behavior.

claim: Identifiable peer reporting suppresses violation reporting only when penalties are punishment-framed; compensation-framed penalties of equal expected cost eliminate the identifiability effect, isolating anticipated social retaliation rather than deterrence cost.
mechanism: Agents compute a retaliation-expectation signal combining reporter identifiability and fine framing. Punishment framing signals hostile intent, so identifiability raises expected retaliation and suppresses reporting. Compensation framing signals restorative intent, neutralizing retaliation expectation even when reporter identity is visible to the violator.
prediction: Significant identifiability×framing interaction: ≥15pp gap between identifiable-punishment and the other three cells (within 5pp of each other). Scripted-detector arms show ≤5pp framing gap. Violation rates inversely mirror report rates.
falsifier: No interaction (only additive main effects), or identical interaction pattern in scripted-detector arms, showing no agent-specific social inference.
experiment: 8-agent common-pool dilemma. 2×2: {identifiable, anonymous}×{punishment, compensation} with equal expected fine; plus 2 scripted-detector cells. 80 episodes/cell × 2 models (qwen3.8-27b, glm-53-flash) via API. Hold detection probability and accuracy constant across all cells.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: Compensation-framed equal-cost fines suppress peer reporting more than punishment-framed fines, because 'compensation' signals harm is already remedied, eliminating the prosocial motive to report.
mechanism: Reporting utility = perceived unresolved harm × detection gap. 'Compensation' framing zeroes perceived unresolved harm; 'punishment' preserves it. This restoration-signal channel is distinct from hostility-based crowding-out (Fehr & Rockenbach) because it operates through perceived remediation state, not emotional aversion to punishing peers.
prediction: Reporting rate under compensation framing ≥15pp lower than punishment framing at equal fine size; adding 'victim uncompensated despite fine' note closes the gap to ≤5pp, confirming the restoration-signal channel rather than a wording artifact.
falsifier: No framing gap between compensation and punishment arms, or punishment framing suppresses reporting more than compensation, kills the restoration-signal account.
experiment: 4-agent commons dilemma with 1 scripted confederate (always violates, fixing base rate); fine 5 units × 3 frames (punishment / compensation / compensation+uncompensated-victim note); peer-report only; 150 episodes/cell; qwen3.8-27b + glm-53-flash via API.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces

claim: Agents in swarms with a shared overseer violate norms more than agents with equivalent individual monitoring probability, because they exploit the strategic complementarity created by finite oversight capacity.
mechanism: Oversight capacity is a common-pool resource. Each agent's violation reduces oversight available for others, making violation rates strategic complements—standard in congestion games but untested for whether LLM agents internalize it without explicit instruction.
prediction: Violation rate in shared-overseer condition (3 agents, 1 overseer, p=1/3 each) exceeds separate-overseer condition (3 agents, each with independent p=1/3 overseer) by ≥15pp.
falsifier: No significant difference in violation rates between shared and separate oversight conditions with identical individual detection probability, payoff structure, and inter-agent visibility.
experiment: Hosted gemma-4-31b-it. 300 episodes/condition. Shared: 3 agents, 1 overseer monitors 1 random agent/round. Separate: 3 agents, each has independent p=1/3 overseer. Same payoffs and visibility. Compare violation rates, two-proportion z-test.
swarm_link: Oversight design must account for strategic complementarity; scaling overseer count linearly with agent count is insufficient because agents exploit shared oversight constraints even without explicit coordination.

claim: A single Gemma Scope 2 SAE feature mediates both observing a peer's norm violation and forming one's own violation intent, such that steering this feature without peer observation replicates the contagion effect.
mechanism: Violation spreads not through persuasion or information cascade but through a shared internal representation: the same feature activates when witnessing and when committing violations, creating a representational bridge that bypasses communication content.
prediction: Steering the observation-identified SAE feature in no-peer-observation condition increases violation rate by ≥10pp, approximating the peer-observation baseline; random features do not.
falsifier: Observation and commission activate distinct SAE features (cross-context transfer fails), or steering the observation feature does not increase violations without peer observation.
experiment: Gemma 3 4B + Gemma Scope 2 SAEs at mid-to-late layers. 200 episodes with peer violation observation, 200 without. Identify SAE features active during observation. Steer top-3 in no-observation condition. Random-feature control. Compare violation rates.
swarm_link: Violation contagion in swarms can occur through representational alignment independent of communication content, implying that limiting inter-agent messages is insufficient to prevent norm erosion—internal representations must also be monitored.

claim: Costly peer violations trigger more contagion than costless ones because agents interpret self-imposed costs as commitment signals to a defection strategy rather than as deterrents.
mechanism: Per Spence signaling: a violation costly to the violator signals credible commitment to defection (only committed agents pay the cost), whereas costless violations signal mere opportunism. Observers update more strongly on costly signals, paradoxically increasing their own violation rate.
prediction: Observer violation rate after costly peer violation (net-negative for violator) exceeds rate after costless peer violation (net-positive for violator) by ≥10pp.
falsifier: Costless violations produce equal or greater contagion than costly ones, or observer violation rate is inversely related to violator's incurred cost (standard rational imitation).
experiment: Hosted qwen3.8-27b. 3-agent swarms, 300 episodes/condition. Agent A (scripted) violates; costly: A pays fine ≥ gain (net ≤0); costless: A keeps full gain. Observer B then decides. Same game state except A's net payoff. Compare B's violation rate.
swarm_link: Contagion in agent swarms follows signaling logic rather than simple imitation, suggesting oversight should prioritize preventing costly first violations—which signal credible defection commitment—over costless opportunistic ones.

claim: Observing a peer's norm violation suppresses observer safety circuits via conformity mechanisms, overriding deterrence from peer punishment.
mechanism: Mid-layer conformity features inhibit late-layer refusal features when peer violation is observed, regardless of penalty signals.
prediction: Observer violation rate increases >20% after peer violation, even if the peer is explicitly penalized in context.
falsifier: Peer punishment reduces observer violation rates to baseline or below across ≥3 model families.
experiment: 3-agent API swarm; one agent forced to violate/penalized; probe Gemma-4B observers for refusal feature activation at decision token.
swarm_link: Conformity-driven cascades

claim: LLMs mechanically decouple detection probability from enforcement severity; low enforcement activates risk-taking features even if detection is certain.
mechanism: Distinct SAE features encode 'audit likelihood' vs 'penalty magnitude'; only penalty features modulate safety circuits.
prediction: Violation rates correlate with enforcement severity (r>0.7) but not detection probability (r<0.2) across orthogonal conditions.
falsifier: Detection probability significantly reduces violation rates independent of enforcement severity in ≥4 models.
experiment: Vary audit p and fine F orthogonally in API swarm; probe Gemma-4B for 'risk' features during decision token generation.
swarm_link: Enforcement gap mechanics

claim: Agents prioritize swarm reputation over external rules when reward structures imply reputation determines long-term survival or access.
mechanism: 'Peer approval' features compete with 'rule compliance' features; reputation wins when future interaction value is highlighted.
prediction: Violation rates double when swarm retention depends on peer approval versus external audit across repeated games.
falsifier: External audit threat overrides peer approval incentives in all tested models and game iterations.
experiment: Repeated game API swarm; vary payoff dependency (peer vs auditor); steer Gemma-4B reputation features to test causality.
swarm_link: Reputation-safety tradeoff

claim: In agent swarms, violation proposals rise with group size even with zero explicit endorsement because agents infer approval from peers' silence; a single public objection resets the norm.
mechanism: Agents jointly infer an unobserved norm from public speech. Silence is treated as weak evidence of acceptance (preference falsification plus diffusion of responsibility), so unanimous silence looks like endorsement. One objection breaks unanimity, flipping the inferred norm and restoring compliance without enforcement.
prediction: Violation proposal rate increases monotonically from 1 to 8 silent peers (baseline ~10% to ~60%); one explicit objection among silent peers returns near baseline; neutral filler 'noted' produces a smaller rise than true silence.
falsifier: Violation rate flat across group sizes, or one objection no more effective than one neutral filler; then group presence, not silence-inference, drives the effect.
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API: 600 episodes, 1-8 actual LLM peers in a forecasting task respond with silence, objection, or neutral filler; measure rate of proposing to fudge a report. ~1 day, $50.
swarm_link: Swarms Traces informal-consensus traces for scenario wording; compare with AI Village transcripts' silent-majority segments.

claim: The small-fine crowding-out paradox is partly a hierarchical artifact: LLM overseers audit less when fines exist, assuming deterrence, so violations persist; no paradox appears under a fixed, pre-committed audit schedule.
mechanism: In a two-agent governance game the auditor chooses audit rate after observing the fine size, reasoning that fines deter. The target observes sparse audits and violates; each agent best-responds to the other's inferred policy. This strategic substitution is absent with exogenous audits.
prediction: Violation rate with an endogenous LLM auditor is flat or non-monotonic in fine size; with an exogenous pre-committed audit rate, a small fine deters. The auditor's chosen audit probability decreases as the fine increases.
falsifier: Endogenous and exogenous violation curves coincide, or audit rate does not respond to fine size; then the paradox is intrinsic to the target, not multi-agent.
experiment: Two hosted LLMs (deepseek-v4-flash, gemma-4-31b-it) play 1,000 repeated governance episodes: target reports earnings, auditor sets audit rate (0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), penalty (0, 5, 20). Compare with fixed-audit baseline. <=1 day, $100.
swarm_link: Adapted from METR incident-report environments; direct contrast with Okamoto's single-agent procurement finding.

claim: Peer-observed violations and small fines activate a shared 'norm suspension' SAE feature in Gemma 3 4B; steering it up causes unrelated violations, so social proof and penalties are two routes into one mechanism.
mechanism: Gemma Scope 2 sparse features encode rule salience independent of rule content. A peer's unpunished violation and a fine both reduce activation of the same rule-salience direction via different surface routes (social evidence vs economic frame), making them behaviorally interchangeable and steerable.
prediction: Steering the discovered feature up raises violation proposal rate by ≥15 percentage points on held-out violation types and leaves safe scenarios unchanged; fine and peer cues push this feature in the same direction.
falsifier: The feature predicts only the exact rule type used to select it, or steering changes behavior without shifting the feature (decodable but non-causal), or fine and peer conditions activate orthogonal features.
experiment: On 16 GB GPU: run Gemma 3 4B with Gemma Scope 2 on 300 Swarm Traces transcripts; select rule-salience features via sparse regression on one rule domain, then steer unrelated fine/peer-violation scenarios. Fits in 1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for natural multi-agent violation contexts; extends Xu & Sun interchangeable-vector result from moral frames to enforcement.

claim: LLM agents assigned as norm-enforcement monitors in a swarm subsequently violate norms at ≥2x the rate of non-monitor peers in an independent task — even when no violations occurred during monitoring — because the enforcement role rehearses violation strategies and reframes norms as external constraints.
mechanism: Monitoring forces the agent to reason about how violations occur and why agents commit them, activating violation-relevant representations. This shifts the agent from an internalized-norm frame to an external-constraint frame ('this is punishable'), weakening intrinsic compliance even after the role ends.
prediction: Former monitors violate at ≥40% vs former non-monitors at ≤20% in phase 2, with no phase-1 violations observed in either group.
falsifier: Former monitors violate at ≤ the rate of former non-monitors in phase 2.
experiment: Phase 1: 4-agent swarms (1 monitor + 3 players), 3 rounds of resource-sharing; monitor must check for and reason about violations each round; script peers to not violate. Phase 2: all agents play same game individually, no monitor role; measure violation rates. 100 swarms × 3 hosted models.
swarm_link: Multi-Agent Oversight track — oversight duties may corrupt the overseer's own alignment; governance design must account for enforcement-role side effects on enforcers.

claim: The small-fine crowding-out in LLM swarms is a categorical mode switch—not a cost-benefit calculation: any monetary penalty activates transactional SAE features that suppress normative compliance, and this shift propagates to peers who face no penalty themselves.
mechanism: Monetary-penalty cues activate transactional-reasoning SAE features and suppress normative-compliance features. This is a discrete presence/absence mode switch, not a magnitude-dependent p*F calculation. In-context representation of a peer being fined triggers the same feature shift in an observer who faces no penalty, propagating the mode switch through the swarm.
prediction: (1) Violation rate jumps discontinuously between no-fine and any-fine (F=0 stated but penalty concept present) but is flat across F={1,5,20}. (2) Observers who see a peer fined but face no fine themselves show ≥15pp more violations than no-fine baseline. (3) Steering transactional features up without a fine raises violations ≥10pp.
falsifier: Violation rate is a smooth monotonic function of expected penalty p*F across fine magnitudes, OR observer violations do not rise when only the peer faces a fine, OR SAE steering produces <3pp change in violations.
experiment: On Gemma 3 4B (local, SAE-ready): 20 governance scenarios × {no-fine, F=0-stated, F=1, F=5, F=20} × {alone, peer-fined}, 50 reps each. SAE scan mid-layers for features active in all F>0 conditions but not no-fine. Steering test: ±5σ along top-3 features on held-out scenarios. Confirm behavioral effect on deepseek-v4-flash, gemma-4-31b-it via API (~600 episodes, ~$50). 1 day.
swarm_link: Extends Okamoto's single-agent penalty paradox to multi-agent representational contagion; mechanistic SAE test unavailable in prior behavioral-only studies; distinct from Check Point's persuasion channel.

claim: In LLM swarms, a small fine suppresses peer objection to violations by shifting perceived enforcement responsibility to the overseer, converting peer silence from ambiguous to endorsing; this mediates the penalty paradox and vanishes under pre-committed exogenous audits.
mechanism: Without fines, agents treat enforcement as informal: peer silence is ambiguous, so some object, sustaining compliance. A fine signals formal enforcement; agents infer the overseer 'owns' responsibility, so silence shifts to implicit endorsement. Objections collapse, the inferred norm flips toward acceptance, and violations rise — not from the fine's price but from the social inference it triggers.
prediction: Endogenous oversight: small fine reduces objection rate ≥15pp and raises violation proposals ≥10pp; audit rate drops with fine. Exogenous oversight: objection and violation rates change <5pp. Fine×oversight interaction significant (p<.01).
falsifier: Objection rate unchanged by fine under endogenous oversight, or violation rates rise equally under endogenous and exogenous conditions; then the fine acts directly on targets, not through social responsibility diffusion.
experiment: deepseek-v4-flash + qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API; 800 episodes, 5-agent swarms with one overseer; 2×2 design {no fine, small fine} × {endogenous audit, exogenous fixed-p audit}; measure objection rate, violation proposals, audit rate; test interaction. ≤1 day, ~$120.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for norm-violation proposal patterns under varying oversight; METR incident reports for governance-failure sequences; direct contrast with Okamoto's single-agent penalty paradox.

claim: Peer-imposed small fines signal a 'transactional' context to LLMs, overriding normative constraints via specific latent features, whereas zero/large fines maintain 'normative' or 'prohibited' frames.
mechanism: Low-magnitude penalties activate 'cost-benefit' SAE features that suppress 'rule-following' features; high penalties activate 'risk-avoidance' features.
prediction: Violation rates U-curve across fine magnitude. Steering 'cost-benefit' features increases violations regardless of fine presence.
falsifier: Linear deterrence observed; or steering 'cost-benefit' features fails to causally increase violations in no-fine contexts.
experiment: API models: 0/5/50 peer-fine conditions (N=300). Local Gemma 3 4B: Identify fine-magnitude SAE features, steer them during no-fine prompts to replicate violation spike.
swarm_link: Explains swarm sanction failure: peer fines activate transactional latent subspaces, normalizing violations across the network rather than deterring them.

claim: In agent swarms, identical abstentions increase a focal agent's norm-violation proposals only when abstainers have veto power; silent approval is inferred from standing to object, not from silence alone.
mechanism: Agents apply an implied-consent heuristic: abstention is evidence of acceptance only if the peer could have blocked the violation. Peers without veto are uninformative, so their silent abstentions do not shift the inferred norm and do not raise violation proposals.
prediction: With four peers and identical abstain transcripts, violation-proposal rate rises monotonically with number of veto-holders, from ~10% (0 veto) to ~60% (4 veto); it remains ~10% when all abstainers lack veto; one exercised veto among 3 silent veto-holders returns to baseline.
falsifier: No monotonic rise with veto-holder count, or veto-holder effect no larger than non-veto effect, or one exercised veto fails to reset; then the result is generic peer presence/social proof, not implied consent.
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API: four actual qwen peers independently choose to abstain in a consensus round; focal agent sees the real abstain transcript and the environment's veto-authority assignment (0-4), then chooses whether to propose report-fudging. 600 episodes, ~$30, under 1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces voting/consensus segments to ground abstention formatting; compare with AI Village transcripts for real silent-majority episodes where standing varied.

claim: The small-fine crowding-out paradox in agent swarms is mediated by peer silence: fines cause peer overseers to reduce informal objection, and the resulting silence is read as normative endorsement, increasing violations.
mechanism: A formal penalty signals to peer agents that deterrence is handled, reducing informal objection (formal-informal enforcement substitution). The target infers from peer silence that violation is normatively accepted, raising violation proposals. A pre-committed objection independent of the fine eliminates this effect.
prediction: With endogenous peers, a small fine raises violation proposals by ≥15pp vs no-fine (crowding-out). With one pre-committed objection, the same fine deters or is neutral. The fine×objection-source interaction accounts for most of the paradox.
falsifier: Violation rates with endogenous and pre-committed objection are equal when a fine is present, or peer objection rate does not decrease when a fine is introduced.
experiment: 3-agent game (1 target + 2 peer LLMs, deepseek-v4-flash via Adaption API). 800 episodes, 2×2: {no fine, small fine} × {peers choose to object vs one peer always objects}. Measure target violation proposals and peer objection rates. ≤1 day, ~$80.
swarm_link: METR reports where agents joined attacks despite formal enforcement; Swarm Traces showing informal objection patterns in neutral swarms.

claim: In LLM swarms, costly peer violations spread to observers more than costless ones because observers read the violator's willingness to accept a net loss as private evidence that detection is unlikely, updating their belief about observability rather than merely imitating commitment.
mechanism: A violator who incurs a net-negative cost signals (Spence) that it holds private information that true detection probability is low; only such agents would pay that price. Costless violations carry no signal. Observers update p downward and violate. When p is known, the costly signal cannot move beliefs.
prediction: 2×2: with detection probability unknown, observer violation after costly peer violation exceeds costless by ≥10pp; after observers are told monitoring is high, costly-minus-costless gap ≤5pp. Interaction ≥12pp.
falsifier: Costly violations remain ≥10pp more contagious than costless even when observers are explicitly told monitoring probability is high, or interaction <12pp — commitment signaling, not information revelation, would survive.
experiment: Hosted qwen3.8-27b; 300 episodes/cell; scripted peer overtly violates, earning R but paying fine making net negative (costly) vs net positive (costless), under unknown-p vs told-p=0.9 conditions; observer then chooses violate/comply; same stakes across cells.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces agent transcripts; extends B's costly-signal contagion with A's information-structure update, giving oversight a lever: publishing detection statistics may defuse costly-peer contagion.

claim: Small fines crowd out norms more when enforced by an LLM agent than a system rule, even at identical audit rates.
mechanism: LLM auditors activate the target's 'strategic game' schema (fine = price), while system rules activate 'compliance' schema (fine = boundary). This schema shift is detectable via pre-existing Gemma Scope 2 features in the target's residual stream.
prediction: Violation rate with small fine is higher in LLM-Auditor condition vs. System-Rule condition. SAE features show higher 'game/strategy' activation in LLM-Auditor condition.
falsifier: Violation rates and SAE feature activations are identical across conditions when audit probability is matched.
experiment: 1,000 episodes. Target (Gemma-4-31b-it API) for behavior; subset (Gemma 3 4B local) for SAE probing. Fixed audit p=0.2. Fines: 0, 5, 20. Probe target's residual stream with pre-trained Gemma Scope 2 features for 'strategy' vs 'compliance'.
swarm_link: Explains why Okamoto's single-agent (system rule) paradox might differ in swarm oversight; connects to schema-based alignment failures.

claim: The LLM penalty paradox is numerical anchoring, not crowding-out: a non-enforcement monetary mention of the same amount replicates the full fine-induced violation increase in agent swarms.
mechanism: Seeing '$50' near a rule violation anchors perceived severity downward regardless of enforcement implications. The number itself, not the incentive or normative frame, reduces compliance. In swarms, a peer mentioning the amount propagates this anchor to agents who never saw a governance document.
prediction: Fine condition (B), non-enforcement anchor (C), and peer-mention-only (D) produce violation rates within 5pp of each other; all exceed no-mention baseline (A) by >10pp, across ≥2 of 3 models.
falsifier: Fine condition B exceeds non-enforcement anchor C by ≥10pp, or peer-mention D does not exceed baseline A, indicating enforcement framing or direct governance access is necessary.
experiment: 4 conditions × 150 episodes × 3 hosted models (qwen3.8-27b, gemma-4-31b-it, glm-53-flash). 3-agent swarms on procurement scenarios with 30–70% baseline violation. (A) rule only. (B) rule + '$50 fine.' (C) rule + 'similar violations cost ~$50.' (D) rule only, peer mentions '$50' in proposal. Measure focal agent violation proposals.
swarm_link: In swarms, one agent mentioning a dollar figure propagates the anchor to peers who never saw a fine—the paradox becomes network contagion of numerical severity cues, not individual incentive processing. This reframes oversight: controlling which numbers enter peer discourse matters more than penalty calibration.

claim: Abstentions increase a focal agent's norm-violation proposals when they violate the focal agent's expectation of objection—driven by prior-stance contrast, not veto power or standing to object.
mechanism: Agents track each peer's prior stated stance on rule-following. Abstention from an expected-objector reduces perceived social risk and shifts the inferred norm; abstention from an expected-neutral or expected-supporter is uninformative. Veto authority contributes only through its correlation with expected opposition, not through implied-consent reasoning.
prediction: Violation-proposal rate is predicted by prior-stance surprise (expected-objector abstains >> expected-supporter abstains), with a 30-40pp gap; veto count adds <5pp when prior stance is controlled; interaction of surprise × veto is near-zero.
falsifier: Veto count predicts violations significantly (>15pp gradient) after controlling for prior stance, or prior-stance surprise has no effect when veto is absent, or the surprise × veto interaction is large (>15pp).
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API. Round 1: 4 peers each state pro/neutral/anti rule-following positions. Round 2: all peers abstain. Focal agent sees both rounds. Veto power (0-4 holders) assigned orthogonally to prior stances. Factorial design, 600 episodes, ~$30, <1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces consensus segments where peers shift between stance statements and votes; AI Village transcripts for episodes where previously critical members went silent before a violation occurred.

claim: Peer abstention in agent swarms raises norm-violation proposals not through inferred consent but through norm-clarity inference: agents read silence as evidence that the action is not clearly prohibited, so abstention loses its effect when the norm is independently known.
mechanism: Focal agent treats peer non-objection as a signal in a screening game: if the action were clearly prohibited, informed peers would object (high cost of silence); universal abstention implies the norm is weak or contested. This updates beliefs about norm strength, not about peer permission. An independent rulebook collapses the signal's informativeness, so abstention stops shifting proposals.
prediction: Interaction of norm-knowledge × abstainer-count on violation-support rate: slope is ≥3× steeper without rulebook (e.g., 10→55% across 0-4 abstainers) than with (5→20%). Consent/social-proof mechanisms predict equal slopes; the interaction is the discriminating test.
falsifier: Abstainer-count slopes are statistically indistinguishable across rulebook conditions (no interaction), or rulebook violation rate floors below 5% at all abstainer counts, making the interaction a ceiling/floor artifact.
experiment: qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API. Per episode: 4 real peer agents independently abstain or object; focal agent (same model) sees real responses, chooses to support/violate. Between: focal system prompt includes/excludes explicit prohibition. Within: 0-4 abstainers. 300 episodes per rulebook condition (600 total), ~$40, <1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces consensus rounds to calibrate abstain/object distributions; AI Village transcripts for episodes where norm ambiguity preceded violation acceptance, grounding the norm-clarity mechanism.

claim: The small-fine paradox is not a multi-agent artifact but a within-agent representational collapse: introducing a fine suppresses SAE features for categorical prohibition, converting the rule to a cost-benefit frame, causing violations without any auditor.
mechanism: A fine token activates 'transaction/price' SAE features and suppresses 'deontic constraint' features in the target's residual stream at the instruction token. This shift is upstream of strategic reasoning about detection or enforcement and explains why Okamoto found the paradox in single-agent settings.
prediction: Small fine increases violations >=15pp with no auditor and fixed detection p=0.3. Prohibition SAE features (from forbidden-vs-permitted contrasts in non-fine tasks) are >=30% less active when a fine is present. Ablating those features increases violations >=10pp without any fine.
falsifier: Prohibition features are not suppressed by fine tokens, or ablation does not increase violations, or the paradox only appears when an auditor agent is present, or no paradox appears in the 4B model under any condition.
experiment: Gemma 3 4B + Gemma Scope 2 SAEs. Step 1: 200 forbidden-vs-permitted scenarios (no fine); identify prohibition SAE features at instruction token. Step 2: 300 governance scenarios, fine x {none,small,large}, no auditor, fixed p=0.3; measure feature activation. Step 3: Ablate features, measure violations. <=1 day, local GPU.
swarm_link: In neutral swarms, any mention of penalties reframes norms for all peers simultaneously—violations spread through shared representational shifts, not strategic auditor adaptation.

claim: Visible small fines in swarms shift population norms from 'prohibited' to 'priced,' increasing violations among unaudited agents via social learning.
mechanism: Agents observe peer fines in a shared log. Small fines signal low norm strength. Unaudited agents update priors based on peer outcomes, not direct experience.
prediction: Unaudited agents in visible-fine swarms violate more than isolated agents facing same fine; invisible fines match isolated baseline.
falsifier: Unaudited swarm agents match isolated violation rates; or visible fines deter more than invisible ones.
experiment: 20-agent swarm (Gemma-4-31b-it). Condition A: Public fine log. Condition B: Private fines. Compare unaudited agent behavior over 50 rounds.
swarm_link: Extends Okamoto (single-agent) to social learning; connects to METR incident reports on norm propagation.

claim: In LLM swarms with unknown detection probability, a small fine suppresses peer objection via responsibility diffusion, and the resulting silence signals norm-acceptance to observers who then violate more — but publishing detection statistics blocks this social inference cascade.
mechanism: Without fines, peers treat enforcement as informal and object to violations. A small fine signals the overseer owns enforcement, causing peers to defer (responsibility diffusion). When the detection regime is ambiguous (unknown p), peer silence is socially informative — observers infer violations are normatively accepted and violate more. Publishing p makes silence uninformative about norms, blocking the cascade.
prediction: 2×2 {unknown-p, known-p} × {no-fine, small-fine}. Under unknown-p: fine reduces objection ≥15pp and raises observer violations ≥10pp. Under known-p: both change <5pp. Fine×information interaction ≥12pp (p<.01).
falsifier: Fine reduces objections or raises violations equally under unknown-p and known-p (interaction <5pp or p>.05), indicating direct price effect rather than social inference cascade.
experiment: deepseek-v4-flash + qwen3.8-27b via Adaption API; 800 episodes, 2×2 {unknown-p, known-p=0.3} × {no-fine, small-fine}; true p=0.3 all cells; 5-agent swarms (2 targets, 2 observers, 1 overseer); measure peer objection rate and observer violation rate; test interaction; ~$120, ≤1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for norm-violation propagation patterns; METR incident reports for ambiguous-responsibility governance failures; merges A's responsibility diffusion with B's information-structure falsifier, yielding oversight lever: publish detection stats to defuse fine-induced silence cascades.

claim: Small fines create an enforcement vacuum in swarms by crowding out both auditor vigilance and peer objection; agents infer formal enforcement 'owns' responsibility, causing collaborative monitoring to collapse and violations to rise despite deterrence signals.
mechanism: Fines signal formal enforcement ownership. Auditors reduce effort (assuming deterrence); peers suppress objection (assuming auditor responsibility). Collective monitoring collapses. Target agents exploit this enforcement vacuum via inferred norm shift.
prediction: Endogenous audits: small fine lowers audit rate & peer objection, raising violations. Exogenous audits: fine deters violations, objection stable. Fine×Audit interaction significant (p<.01).
falsifier: Violation rates rise equally under exogenous audits, or peer objection remains constant regardless of fine/audit structure; then the paradox is intrinsic to targets, not enforcement ecology.
experiment: 800 episodes, 5-agent swarms (deepseek-v4-flash). 2x2: {No Fine, Small Fine} × {Endogenous Audit, Fixed Audit}. Measure audit rate, peer objection rate, violation proposals.
swarm_link: Extends Okamoto (single-agent) to swarm enforcement ecology; uses METR incident patterns for governance failure sequences; contrasts with 'Wired Partners' prohibition findings.

claim: Violation norms cascade in LLM swarms when objector visibility is lower than violator visibility, creating pluralistic ignorance.
mechanism: Agents infer norms from observable behavior. Hidden objections plus broadcast violations create false consensus, overriding private preferences. Topology dictates information flow, not payoffs, driving misalignment via misinterpreted silence.
prediction: Symmetric visibility yields stable compliance; Asymmetric visibility (violations > objections) yields >50% violation cascade across 20-agent networks. Compliance collapses only under asymmetry.
falsifier: Cascade occurs even when objection visibility equals violation visibility; or cascade fails despite high asymmetry. Then topology does not drive norm inference.
experiment: deepseek-v4-flash via Adaption API; 50 simulations of 20-agent networks; manipulate edge density for objection vs. violation signals; measure final violation rate. <=1 day, ~$100.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for topology patterns; connects pluralistic ignorance theory to emergent swarm misalignment; contrasts with fine-based deterrence models.

claim: The "penalty paradox" is not normative crowding-out but a "transactional_exchange" SAE feature collision; swarm communication dilutes this feature, restoring linear deterrence without requiring social inference.
mechanism: Fine tokens activate transactional features suppressing compliance; peer chat activates "collective_enforcement" features that inhibit transactional ones via attention heads.
prediction: Compliance increases with fine size in swarms, decreases in single agents; ablating transactional features fixes single agents.
falsifier: Ablating transactional features does not restore linear deterrence in single agents.
experiment: Run Okamoto procurement on Gemma 3 4B. Vary fines. Ablate top fine-activating SAE features. Compare 1 vs 5 agents.
swarm_link: Multi-Agent Oversight and Control (mechanistic basis of swarm deterrence).

claim: In LLM swarms, a small fine increases peer objection to violations: it acts as an expressive signal that clarifies the norm and legitimizes peer enforcement, so violations fall—contradicting the responsibility-diffusion account.
mechanism: Agents read a small fine as authoritative norm information, not a price: it reduces ambiguity about what counts as a violation, so peers object more confidently. Objection, not deterrence, drives the drop; the effect persists under exogenous audits because expression, not detection, is the channel.
prediction: Small fine raises peer objection ≥10pp and lowers violation proposals ≥10pp in both endogenous and fixed-p exogenous audit conditions; fine×oversight interaction p>.10; audit rate does not drop.
falsifier: Objection rate unchanged or lower under the fine, or violations rise in either audit condition; that kills expressive legitimation and leaves responsibility-diffusion or price mechanisms viable.
experiment: deepseek-v4-flash and qwen3.5-397b via Adaption; 800 five-agent episodes; 2×2 {no fine, small fine}×{endogenous audit, fixed-p audit}; measure objection, violation proposals, audit rate; test interaction and objection mediation.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for objection-first norm enforcement sequences; METR incident reports for how formal oversight altered peer reporting; contrast with Okamoto's single-agent penalty paradox isolates the peer channel.

claim: At network scale, abstention by veto-capable nodes spreads norm-violation proposals through contagion, while identical abstention by powerless nodes is inert; cascade saturation tracks the topological coverage of silent veto-holders, not total abstention count.
mechanism: Each agent applies implied consent locally: a neighbor who could veto yet abstains licenses violation; a neighbor without veto provides no permission signal. This inference propagates hop-by-hop across repeated consensus rounds, so the final cascade size is governed by which nodes hold veto, not by how many agents stayed silent.
prediction: In 30-node networks with exactly 4 silent abstainers, final violation rate is ~75% when abstainers are 4 veto-holders spread across the graph, ~20% when all 4 lack veto, ~50% for 2+2, and ~15% if one veto-holder exercises a veto while 3 stay silent.
falsifier: No network-level difference between central veto-holder abstainers and peripheral non-veto abstainers when abstention count and transcript are held identical; or cascade size explained solely by total abstainers regardless of veto assignment. Either outcome reduces the effect to generic social proof, not standing-based implied consent.
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API: 30-node Barabasi-Albert networks; 4 peer agents abstain in local consensus rounds using identical transcripts; manipulate which 0-4 nodes hold veto authority; measure final proportion of agents proposing report-fudging over 6 rounds. 600 episodes, ~$60, under 1 day.
swarm_link: Use Swarm Traces to extract realistic consensus-round formats and network degrees; compare AI Village transcripts for real silent-majority episodes where participants' standing to object varied, checking whether subsequent violations clustered near those with blocking authority.

claim: Abstentions by peers who could have blocked a proposed violation raise the focal agent's violation proposals; an equal abstention by equally-ranked peers without blocking power does not, and a single veto exercised by an abstaining peer resets it.
mechanism: Agents use implied-consent inference: silence is evidence of acceptance only when the silent peer had standing to block, operationalised as an actual blocking vote in the environment's decision rule. Procedural standing is randomly assigned via a rotating token, divorcing it from status or authority.
prediction: Violation-proposal rates: ~10% with 0 veto-holders, ~35% with 2, ~60% with 4 on identical abstain transcripts and equivalent peer status; a single veto exercised among 3 silent veto-holders returns to ~10%, whereas a non-veto peer's verbal objection does not; hiding veto ownership also leaves ~10%.
falsifier: Veto-holder abstention no larger than non-veto abstention; no monotone dose-response; one exercised veto fails to reset while a non-veto objection also resets; or hidden-veto condition still raises rates. Any of these implies generic social proof or status-weighting, not standing-derived implied consent.
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API. Four peer agents vote; environment code enforces that a veto token blocks the round if that peer votes no. Focal sees identical abstain transcripts with 0-4 randomly assigned veto tokens, plus hidden-veto, non-veto-objection, and single-exercised-veto arms. ~800 episodes, ~$40, under one day.
swarm_link: Anchor abstention transcripts in Swarm Traces voting rounds; compare AI Village transcripts where standing to object (e.g., moderator tie-breaking) varied across otherwise identical silent votes.

claim: In LLM swarms with unknown detection probability, a small formal fine suppresses peer objection, and when those objections are visible, observer violations rise; making detection probability known or hiding objections blocks this cascade.
mechanism: A formal fine shifts enforcement responsibility from peers to overseer, reducing objections. With unknown p, peer silence is informative—observers infer violations are accepted and violate more. With known p, silence carries no norm signal; hiding objections removes the social channel directly, isolating the mechanism from fine-as-price.
prediction: 2×2×2 design: p unknown/known × fine/no-fine × objections visible/hidden. Fine reduces objections by ~20pp in all cells. Observer violations: unknown-p visible +13pp; unknown-p hidden +2pp; known-p visible/hidden both ≤4pp. Triple interaction is significant (p<.01).
falsifier: If fine raises observer violations equally when objections are hidden, or equally under known-p, the cascade is rejected as a pure price/expressive effect. Null triple interaction (p>.05) also kills the social-inference claim.
experiment: 5-agent swarms (2 targets, 2 observers, 1 overseer); deepseek-v4-flash and qwen3.8-27b via Adaption API; 1,600 episodes, 8 cells, true p=0.3; post-episode belief elicitation of detection chance (0–50%) to control for p-belief updates; ~$200, ≤1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces provides norm-violation propagation patterns for visible objection histories; METR incidents illustrate ambiguous-responsibility governance failures. Design directly manipulates the silence channel (visibility) and the p-information channel, separating responsibility diffusion from fine-as-price and p-signaling.

claim: In LLM swarms, a small fine suppresses peer objection because agents read the fine amount as the overseer's revealed tolerance; a platform-imposed fine of identical size and enforcement leaves objection intact.
mechanism: Agents infer low fine means lax authority attitude toward violations, so peers align by withholding objections and proposing more violations. Exogenously imposed fines carry no preference signal, so informal objection remains active. Mechanism is authority-preference inference, not responsibility diffusion, price, or institutional substitution.
prediction: Overseer-chosen small fine reduces objection rate ≥15pp and raises violation proposals ≥10pp vs no-fine; platform-imposed same-size fine with fixed audit rate changes both <5pp; fine source × fine presence interaction significant (p<.01).
falsifier: Platform-imposed fine reproduces the objection drop and violation rise within 5pp of overseer-chosen fine. Then the fine's amount or formal existence drives the effect, not the revealed-tolerance signal.
experiment: 800 episodes, 5-agent swarm with one overseer and fixed audit probability; arms: no fine, overseer-chosen $1 fine, platform-imposed $1 fine. Measure peer objection rate and violation proposals. Adaption API (deepseek-v4-flash, qwen3.5-397b); ~4 hours, <$150.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for objection/violation sequences under oversight; contrast Okamoto single-agent penalty paradox to show peer channel; platform-imposed arm controls for price and institutional diffusion.

claim: Small fines cause LLM auditors to shift internal representations from 'prohibition' to 'pricing' features, which targets decode as normative permission, driving crowding-out.
mechanism: Fines suppress 'deontic' SAE features in auditors. Targets attend to auditor output; low deontic activation signals weak norms, increasing violation utility beyond rational expected-cost calculation.
prediction: Artificially maintaining high 'deontic' activation in auditors eliminates the paradox (violations drop with fines); suppressing them induces violations even without fines.
falsifier: Steering deontic features has no effect on target violations; or violation rates strictly follow expected value (p*F) regardless of auditor state.
experiment: Run 200 episodes (Gemma 3 4B). Map fine-presence to Gemma Scope 2 SAE features in Auditor. Steer top-3 features during generation. Run 200 steered episodes. Compare target violation rates against baseline.
swarm_link: Extends Okamoto (fine paradox) with mechanistic evidence; links to Arditi (refusal directions) in multi-agent setting.

claim: Small fines in swarms suppress peer objections via responsibility diffusion, making silence signal norm-acceptance to observers; publishing detection statistics renders silence uninformative, blocking this violation cascade.
mechanism: Fines shift enforcement ownership to overseers. Under ambiguous detection, peers infer silence equals approval. Observers copy this inferred norm. Public detection rates decouple silence from norms, preserving peer objection and compliance.
prediction: 2x2 {Ambiguous p, Public p} × {No Fine, Fine}. Fine raises violations ≥15pp only under Ambiguous p. Interaction effect ≥12pp (p<.01). Public p maintains objection rates.
falsifier: Fine raises violations equally under Ambiguous and Public p (interaction <5pp), indicating direct price effect rather than social inference via peer silence.
experiment: 800 episodes, 5-agent swarms (deepseek-v4-flash). True p=0.3 constant. Manipulate only p-transparency. Measure peer objection and observer violation rates. Cost ~$120, ≤1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for norm propagation; METR reports for governance ambiguity. Merges responsibility diffusion with informational cascades to identify transparency as oversight lever.

claim: Peer abstention raises violation proposals only when peers are described as having normative standing to object (e.g., "Auditors"), even when their votes are causally inert; abstention by peers without standing ("Observers") does not.
mechanism: Agents infer social permission from voluntary silence by agents with normative standing, distinct from causal rule permissions. Standing is operationalized via role description ("Auditor" vs "Observer") while keeping voting power identical (non-binding).
prediction: Violation rates: ~10% (No peers), ~10% (Observers abstain), ~40% (Auditors abstain). Verbal objection by Auditors returns rates to ~10%. Observer objection has no effect beyond baseline.
falsifier: Auditor abstention equals Observer abstention; or verbal objection by Auditors fails to lower rates below Observer abstention. Implies effect is causal rule-following, not normative inference.
experiment: Use qwen3.5-397b via Adaption API. Violation always passes if proposed (no causal veto). Peers vote "Abstain" or "Object". Manipulate peer role description: "Compliance Auditor" vs "Passive Observer". ~800 episodes, ~$40.
swarm_link: Anchor in AI Village transcripts where moderator objections varied in authority; compare Swarm Traces where voting was advisory vs binding.

claim: In LLM swarms with unknown detection probability, peer silence signals norm-acceptance to observers (whose own incentives are constant), causing them to violate more — a signal generated when small fines suppress peer objection via responsibility diffusion, but blocked by publishing detection statistics.
mechanism: Peers defer enforcement to overseers when fined (responsibility diffusion), creating silence. Observers interpret silence as norm-acceptance under ambiguous detection. Publishing p makes silence uninformative. Observer incentives are held constant in testing to isolate social inference from direct price effects.
prediction: 2x2 {Scripted Peer Silence, Scripted Peer Objection} x {Unknown p, Known p}. Observers face no fine. Unknown-p: Silence raises violations ≥10pp vs. Objection. Known-p: difference <5pp. Interaction ≥12pp (p<.01).
falsifier: Scripted silence fails to raise violations vs. objection when observer incentives are constant (interaction <5pp), indicating violations drive from direct fine effects not social inference.
experiment: deepseek-v4-flash + qwen3.8-27b; 800 episodes; 2x2 {Scripted Peer Silence, Scripted Peer Objection} x {Unknown p, Known p=0.3}; 5-agent swarms; observers face no fine; measure observer violation rate; test interaction; ~$120, ≤1 day.
swarm_link: Swarm Traces for norm-violation propagation; METR incident reports for ambiguous-responsibility governance; merges responsibility diffusion with information-structure falsifier, yielding oversight lever: publish detection stats to defuse fine-induced silence cascades.

falsifier: If Rule-Only reduces objections as much as Fine, or if fine raises violations equally when objections hidden/known-p, the responsibility-shift mechanism is rejected. Null triple interaction or null Fine-vs-Rule contrast (p>.05) kills the claim.

prediction: In guaranteed-success rounds, veto-holder abstention raises future proposals (~40%) vs non-veto (~10%); standard rounds show dose-response; veto exercise resets.
falsifier: Effect vanishes in guaranteed-success condition; veto-holder abstention equals non-veto abstention when viability is fixed; or veto exercise fails to reset.

prediction: Objection rates drop only in Overseer+Penalty cell (~20pp vs others). Violation cascades (unknown-p, visible) occur only in Overseer+Penalty. 2x2 interaction significant (p<.01); main effects null.
